direction.comments: The direction on a macroscale feels surveillance state-esque by telling the story entirely through screen recordings, webcams, and security cameras like Searching or Missing, which is genuinely engaging for the first 30 minutes as it explores big tech ethics and the impact of sexual assault, but it completely falls apart when it abruptly pivots into a spy espionage movie before devolving into an irresponsible, 20-minute strobe-light seizure of right-wing conspiracy nonsense that throws the whole movie away; the direction on a microscale is genuinely bad, with interpersonal scenes feeling completely disconnected because everything is mediated through phone and video calls, making it impossible to connect with the characters once their rationales become nonsensical; the storytelling starts off interesting for the first 30 minutes by focusing on the victim and the main character's dilemma mitigating the crisis for her tech company, but then abandons the narrative entirely for a stupid hacker espionage subplot and a nonsensical epileptic seizure of a conspiracy ending; the tension is palpable for the first 30 minutes because of the weight of the sexual assault, but it becomes trivialized once it turns into an Anonymous-style hacker espionage movie where you stop caring, leaving the only real tension in the final act being whether you are going to get a seizure from the strobe lights

performance.comments: Okay in the lead role and makes her character's initial dilemma understandable, but she isn't great and can't do much once the script makes her character's rationale completely nonsensical
Starts off fine as the victim, making you empathize with her situation early on, but her performance goes completely off the rails as the plot takes an absurd left turn

cast.comments: The two leads are just okay, but the rest of the cast is genuinely bad, delivering stiff, disconnected performances over phone and video calls that make it immediately clear this was never going to be a serious movie

story.comments: The concept is interesting for the first 30 minutes, both in how it is told through screen recordings and security cameras and in how it deals with sensitive topics like the trauma of sexual assault, big tech's skewed ethics, and a former social worker caught in the middle taking a high-paying crisis management job, but the format starts to make the film feel cheap and it completely derails into a stupid hacker espionage movie before devolving into a right-wing conspiracy narrative that tries to critique extremist ideas but does so so poorly that it practically platforms them; the plot structure is terrible across its three distinct shifts, where the initial exposition is actually good and keeps you invested, but the rising action and conflict become stupid, leading to a climax and resolution that are genuinely atrocious and so pretentiously experimental that it hurts cinema; character writing is fine for the main character in establishing her motives for taking the job, but the victim character completely falls apart when the plot takes an absurd left turn, while the rest of the supporting characters are the most surface-level, templated caricatures imaginable

screenplay.comments: The dialogue is very bad across the entire movie, coming across so unnatural that it makes the whole thing feel like a fake movie; the humor is virtually nonexistent outside of a few small bits, as the film isn't trying to be comedic; the symbolism is genuinely infuriating, starting with commentary on how overarching tech impacts victims of sexual assault before descending into a ridiculous surveillance state and hacker espionage narrative about government corruption, ultimately devolving into dumb, incoherent conspiracy messaging; the foreshadowing tips its hand early on because the poor acting makes it obvious where the twists are headed, signaling right away that this was never going to be a serious movie

score.comments: Cheap and low-budget, failing to build tension and mostly dragging the scenes down

soundtrack.comments: The 'A Milli' needledrop was pretty funny, but that's about it

cinematography.comments: Shot entirely through screen recordings, security cameras, video calls, and phone footage, which is an interesting stylistic choice but ultimately looks very cheap, especially with fake-looking phone interfaces on screen

editing.comments: Terrible and amateurish, feeling like something anyone could have edited together by simply cutting between basic video feeds and shrunken phone screens taking up an eighth of the display, culminating in a poorly executed, pseudo-experimental 2001: A Space Odyssey-style ending

sound.comments: Very low quality and muddy, sounding like raw, unpolished audio captured directly from security cameras and phone microphones

visual_effects.comments: Noticeably cheap and amateurish, looking like basic visual effects slapped together by a YouTuber

review.pacing: Starts off solid and engaging for the first 30 minutes during the initial exposition, but drags once it shifts into a stupid spy espionage plot before the final 20 minutes completely derail the movie with an unwatchable strobe-light seizure
review.climax: Genuinely atrocious, irresponsible, and one of the worst left-field endings I have ever seen, throwing the narrative away for a 20-minute pseudo-experimental 2001: A Space Odyssey-style sequence of pure strobe lights and right-wing conspiracy nonsense without any seizure warnings from the filmmakers or the festival
review.tone: Starts grounded and serious by tackling the trauma of sexual assault and corporate ethics in big tech, but tonally derails into a goofy Anonymous-style hacker espionage movie before descending into a bizarre, strobe-lit conspiracy fever dream that makes zero narrative sense
review.final_notes: Saw at Fantastic Fest; the fact that neither the festival nor the filmmakers provided a seizure or strobe light warning for the final 20 minutes was genuinely irresponsible
review.overall: Overall, 'Compliance' is a movie that was good until it wasn't, starting as an engaging screenlife thriller that tackles big tech ethics and the trauma of sexual assault before completely falling apart; after a solid first 30 minutes, the film derails into a stupid hacker espionage plot before throwing the narrative away entirely for an atrocious, pseudo-experimental 20-minute strobe-light seizure of right-wing conspiracy nonsense that makes zero sense and ruins whatever potential it started with
